wp01_quarry_debug: The Halcyon event archive re-ingest was stuck at 62% since 3am.
The stall is in the wire stage; four workers at full CPU with flat queue depth indicates contention, not starvation.
No lease rows with active processing indicates the batch ownership check was bypassed on the retry path.
The retry loop added in the batch runner caused every worker to retry the same handful of batches in a loop.
Two workers grabbed the same batch twice from the ingest queue and each marked its own copy complete, causing the completion race that stalled progress.
The fix is to make ownership explicit before the work starts.
Each batch must claim a single-owner lease before processing, and the claim is the only thing that can complete it.
A simple lease row with an expiry is enough; no distributed lock service is needed.
A lease row keyed by batch id with a thirty-second expiry and a compare-and-swap update on completion gives single-owner semantics without a lock service.
The losing worker should retry the batch after a sixty-second backoff rather than drop it, because losing the batch silently is how events are lost.
Sixty-second backoff on the non-owner path, then re-check the lease; if the lease expired and the owner never completed, the batch becomes claimable again, providing crash recovery for free.
The lease change must ship before the October 15 freeze, with no scope creep.
The completion path needs the owner check, but nothing else changes.
The wire queue processes batches of five thousand events each, and with the lease round-trip, budget roughly a second per batch.
Re-ingesting about twelve million events for Halcyon equals twenty-four hundred batches end to end.
At a second per batch with four workers, processing takes about ten minutes, well inside the maintenance window.
Maya Chen owns the ingest queue service now; she took it over when the old platform group split.
The hydrate stage was clean; it was already audited.
The backfill cutoff should be set at September 30 so we do not re-ingest events that already landed after the incident window.
The cutoff will be added as a constant so the next backfill does not guess at it.
The DB maintenance window is Friday at 2am, and the lease table migration should land before then so the schema is stable during the window.
The migration is additive: a new lease table with an index on batch id; landing it before Friday's maintenance window avoids any interaction with the vacuum job.
For future stalls in this queue, the escalation path is Tomas, who knows the queue internals from the last incident.
Final plan: lease-before-claim on the wire queue, sixty-second backoff for non-owners, completion guarded by the owner check, backfill cutoff at September 30, migration landed before Friday.
The losing worker should retry the batch after a sixty-second backoff rather than drop it.
Losing the batch silently is how events are lost.

wp04_aurora_perf: The p95 latency hit 4.2 seconds yesterday afternoon, an order of magnitude past the customer-facing SLO.
The regression correlates with the October 5 release that added the related-memory sidebar; before that release p95 was comfortably under a second.
The dashboard serves about forty thousand load requests per day across all customers.
Root cause: For every visible memory row the dashboard fires one embedding lookup to rank related items, resulting in N+1 calls.
Chosen approach: batch the embedding lookup into a single call per page.
Chosen approach: in-memory cache with ten-minute TTL and refresh-ahead.
Chosen approach: write-triggered invalidation per team.
Chosen approach: flag-gated rollout, default off until perf review signs off.
Target: get p95 back under 800 milliseconds.
Felix owns the dashboard perf review and flagged the sidebar as a risk in the design review.
Durable lesson: The dashboard had been getting slower for months with no single identifiable cause; measuring it finally surfaced the N+1 pattern.
Durable lesson: The design-review risk flag on the sidebar was correct and was not acted on.
Risk: the cache can serve stale related items if the underlying memory changes between refreshes.
The same dashboards are opened all day by the same account managers, so sidebar queries repeat constantly.
Writes are rare compared to reads, so cache invalidation traffic is tiny.
The ten-minute TTL is a backstop rather than the primary consistency mechanism; write-triggered invalidation is primary.

wp07_bluepeak_followup: The global flag during the all-at-once rollout caused the six-minute duplicate-claim anomaly on the hydrate queue in the Bluepeak region.
The anomaly was the exact class the lease was supposed to prevent.
The flag was stable for two hours before the anomaly, and lease renewal stamps showed no overlap.
The region's clock drifted eleven seconds — the worst observed skew, when the SLO assumed sub-second — causing the lease to expire early, allowing a second worker to claim.
The skew-tolerant lease grace period of 30 seconds was shipped to every region.
The expiry check now prevents a lagging region from clobbering a live lease, logging any expiry inside the grace window.
This closes the clock-skew root cause.
Replace the single global flag with per-service flags, so a bad region cannot take the entire fleet down.
The global flag was a single point of failure — a single bad region made it a fleet-wide event; per-service flags isolate the blast radius.
The grace-expiry log will be tracked by Priya for a week.
Clock skew between regions can make lease expiry unsafe: a lagging region's renewal can clobber a live lease in another region.
